title: Mobile technology, data mining and the cloud

pages.c05-p01: Describe how technology supports mobile phone communication: mobile phone masts; cells; handoffs; base station controller; mobile switching centre; and public switched telephone network (PSTN) telephone system
pages.c05-p02: Explain what is meant by data mining
pages.c05-p03: Describe how digital technology can be used in data mining to gather, store, process and analyse large volumes of data
pages.c05-p04: Explain the importance of big data to the operation and competitiveness of organisations in the health, finance and retail sectors
pages.c05-p05: Describe the threats to the privacy of the individual from the use of data mining
pages.c05-p06: Explain what is meant by cloud computing
pages.c05-p07: Explain the terms virtualisation, hosted instances, hosted solutions and clustering
pages.c05-p08: Describe how cloud computing provides services, such as: data storage; email; virtualised software; backup; and remotely hosted applications
pages.c05-p09: Evaluate the use of cloud computing in terms of business benefits and security issues

q.q: Why are mobile phone cells drawn as hexagons?
o: Hexagons stop neighbouring cells from overlapping at all
Hexagons fit together with no gaps, giving full coverage
Hexagons need only one mast for the whole network
Radio waves from a mast spread out in a hexagonal shape
q.why: Tessellating hexagons cover the area completely; neighbouring cells in fact overlap slightly.

q.q: What is a handoff in a mobile phone network?
o: Registering the phone with its home network on switching on
Switching a call from one base station to another as the user moves
Ending a call when the phone moves out of range
Passing a call from the mobile switching centre to the PSTN
q.why: A handoff keeps the call going as the caller crosses from cell to cell.

q.q: Which part of the network connects mobile calls to landlines?
o: The mobile switching centre, through the PSTN
The phone itself, through its SIM card
The base station, through the nearest mast
The base station controller, through a handoff
q.why: The MSC connects to other networks, including the PSTN.

q.q: Why do cities have more, smaller cells than rural areas?
o: Rural areas are not covered by any mobile masts
Buildings in cities block all signals from large cells
More cells allow more calls at once where demand is high
Smaller cells use higher-powered masts than large cells
q.why: Frequencies are reused in non-neighbouring cells, so more cells means more calls at once.

q.q: What does a phone listen for when it is switched on?
o: The System Identification Code broadcast on a control channel
A dial tone sent from the PSTN
A handoff signal from the base station controller
The MAC address of the nearest mobile switching centre
q.why: The phone compares the SID with its programmed one to find its home network.

q.q: What does a phone display if it hears no SID when switched on?
o: Roaming, as it has found another network
No service, as it is out of range
Handoff, as it is moving between cells
Registered, as it has found its home network
q.why: No SID means the phone is out of range.

q.q: Why does the network record which area a phone is in when it registers?
o: So incoming calls can be routed to it
So the phone's SID can be changed
So the phone can be charged for the call
So the mast can increase its power
q.why: The switching centre stores the phone's location in a database to route incoming calls.

q.q: Which part of the network sets up calls and manages handoffs between its base stations?
o: Mobile phone mast
Mobile switching centre
Base station controller
PSTN
q.why: The BSC controls one or more base stations, sets up calls and manages handoffs.

q.q: Which part of the network sets up, routes and releases calls between regions and keeps track of where phones are?
o: Mobile switching centre
Base station controller
Base station
PSTN
q.why: The MSC is the exchange of the mobile network.

q.q: What is the PSTN?
o: The worldwide landline telephone system of wired phones and public exchanges
The radio link between a phone and its nearest mast
The control channel a mobile phone listens to when switched on
The database that records which cell each phone is in
q.why: The public switched telephone network is the landline system, traditionally over copper.

q.q: A caller on a train rings a landline. Which is the correct order the call passes through?
o: Mast and base station, MSC, BSC, PSTN
Mast and base station, BSC, MSC, PSTN
BSC, mast and base station, PSTN, MSC
PSTN, MSC, BSC, mast and base station
q.why: The call goes from the phone to the mast in its cell, the BSC, the MSC and then the PSTN.

q.q: What does a mobile phone mast do?
o: Converts landline calls into text messages
Stores the location of every phone in the country
Routes calls between regions and to landlines
Sends and receives radio signals for its base station
q.why: The mast is a high-powered antenna sending and receiving radio signals.

q.q: How do mobile networks reuse radio frequencies to increase capacity?
o: Every cell uses exactly the same frequencies as its neighbours
Frequencies are reused only when the phone is in a city
Each phone is given its own frequency for the whole network
Each cell reuses frequencies used by cells that are not next to it
q.why: Reusing frequencies in non-neighbouring cells allows many calls at once.

q.q: Which best describes data mining?
o: Backing up large data sets to a provider's servers
Collecting large data sets from social media and sensors
Analysing large data sets to discover patterns and predict trends
Deleting old records to keep a database small
q.why: Data mining is the discovery of patterns in big data to predict future trends.

q.q: What is the difference between big data and data mining?
o: There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
Big data is always structured; data mining only uses unstructured data
Data mining is the data; big data is the process of analysing it
Big data is the data; data mining is the process of analysing it
q.why: Big data is the data itself; data mining is the analysis of it.

q.q: Which three disciplines does data mining combine?
o: Artificial intelligence, statistics and database systems
Hardware design, software design and testing
Networking, robotics and voice recognition
Law, ethics and information security
q.why: Data mining draws on AI, statistics and database systems.

q.q: Why is data mining described as automatic?
o: It deletes data automatically once it has been analysed
It collects data automatically from the user's device
It runs only once a year without any human input
Algorithms search the data rather than a person writing a query
q.why: Algorithms find patterns, rather than a person asking a question they already have.

q.q: Where is the data for data mining usually combined and held?
o: In a flat file
On each user's PC
In a data warehouse
In the PSTN
q.why: Data from several sources is usually combined in a data warehouse.

q.q: Strictly, when does data mining end?
o: When customers have been contacted
When all the data has been deleted
When the organisation has acted on the patterns
When the patterns have been extracted
q.why: What the organisation does with the patterns afterwards is not part of the mining.

q.q: A bank wants to sort loan applicants into 'likely to default' and 'not likely to default' using past examples. Which technique is this?
o: Regression
Association
Clustering
Classification
q.why: Classification assigns records to known categories; clustering discovers new groups.

q.q: A supermarket analyses sales and finds groups such as 'weekday lunch buyers' that it did not know existed. Which technique is this?
o: Anomaly detection
Classification
Association
Clustering
q.why: Clustering discovers groups not known in advance.

q.q: A card is used in Belfast and in Lisbon ten minutes apart. Which data mining technique would flag this?
o: Anomaly detection
Clustering
Regression
Association
q.why: Anomaly (outlier) detection finds records that do not fit the normal pattern.

q.q: Forecasting next week's bread sales from weather and past sales uses which technique?
o: Classification
Clustering
Association
Regression
q.why: Regression predicts a numeric value from other values or past trends.

q.q: What can the summary of patterns produced by data mining be used for?
o: Replacing the data warehouse that the data came from
Registering customers' phones with the mobile network
Feeding other systems, such as a decision support system
Encrypting the original data before it is stored again
q.why: The summarised patterns can feed decision-making systems.

q.q: Which V of big data describes the speed at which data arrives?
o: Value
Variety
Volume
Velocity
q.why: Velocity is speed; volume is amount; variety is the number of data types.

q.q: Which technique finds products that are often bought together?
o: Regression
Anomaly detection
Clustering
Association rule learning
q.why: Association, or market basket analysis, finds items that occur together.

q.q: What is an advantage of object-based storage for big data?
o: It can store only structured tables, which are faster to search
It organises files in deep folder hierarchies across devices
It needs no servers because data is held on users' PCs
Each file has a unique identifier and index, so it is found quickly
q.why: Object storage avoids searching through folder hierarchies.

q.q: Which is an example of machine data?
o: A customer's post on social media
A product review written by a shopper
GPS readings from delivery vans
An online order placed on a website
q.why: Machine data is generated by devices such as RFID readers, GPS and sensors.

q.q: Posts, photos, reviews and sales records are analysed together. Which V of big data does this illustrate?
o: Volume
Validity
Variety
Velocity
q.why: Variety is the number of different types of data.

q.q: Years of smart-card taps on buses and trains illustrate which V of big data?
o: Variety
Volume
Velocity
Visibility
q.why: Volume is the amount of data, from terabytes to petabytes.

q.q: Which is an example of an external source of data for a retailer?
o: The retailer's own product details
Data bought from a market research company
The retailer's own customer details
The retailer's own sales records
q.why: External sources include partners, data suppliers, the internet, government and market research companies.

q.q: Which three sources of big data are described as the most common?
o: Social media, paper records and telephone calls
Transactional data, television and radio broadcasts
Social media, machine data and transactional data
Machine data, printed forms and handwritten notes
q.why: Social media, machine data and transactional data are the three most common sources.

q.q: What does hyperscale storage, used by firms such as Google, involve?
o: Vast numbers of servers, each with direct-attached flash storage
Clustered NAS units with deep hierarchies of folders
Storing the data on each customer's own phone or device
A single large file server with a nightly tape backup
q.why: Hyperscale data centres use huge numbers of servers with fast flash storage.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of clustered network-attached storage (NAS) for big data?
o: Deep folder hierarchies across many devices become hard to manage
It needs every file to be given its own unique identifier
It can only store data collected from social media sites
It cannot be expanded at all once it has been set up
q.why: Clustered NAS scales out easily, but hierarchies across many devices become hard to manage.

q.q: Which technique measures how a change in one variable affects another, such as temperature and ice-cream sales?
o: Classification
Clustering
Summarisation
Regression
q.why: Regression measures how one variable affects another.

q.q: How is the processing of big data made fast enough?
o: Data is only analysed once a year when it stops arriving
The work is split across clusters of servers working in parallel
All data is processed by one powerful server in sequence
Data is printed and analysed by teams of people
q.why: Clusters of servers process parts of the data in parallel, often as it streams in.

q.q: Which technique presents data in a compact, visual form such as a dashboard of sales by region?
o: Association
Regression
Summarisation
Anomaly detection
q.why: Summarisation presents the data compactly and visually.

q.q: How do banks use data mining to fight fraud?
o: By flagging spending that breaks a customer's normal pattern, in real time
By sharing customers' PINs with the card companies each day
By closing any account that makes a payment to an overseas shop
By printing monthly statements for customers to check by hand
q.why: Algorithms learn each customer's normal spending and flag unusual patterns.

q.q: Which is a use of big data in health?
o: Awarding loyalty points to shoppers
Predicting the spread of an epidemic
Optimising the prices of products
Algorithmic trading of shares
q.why: For example, phone location data was used to predict the spread of Ebola in 2014.

q.q: How do retailers use big data to optimise prices?
o: By analysing spending habits, demographics, stock and competitors' prices
By setting one fixed price for each product that never changes
By analysing their staff timesheets and wages, and nothing else
By asking each customer at the till what they want to pay
q.why: Many data sources tracked daily let prices change quickly with the market.

q.q: How did big data help during the 2014 Ebola outbreak?
o: Bank transactions showed which hospitals needed funding
Mobile phone location data tracked movement to predict the spread
Loyalty-card data showed which medicines people bought
Social media posts were used to diagnose individual patients
q.why: Location data showed population movement, helping decide where to place treatment centres.

q.q: How does big data help banks comply with regulations cheaply?
o: Removing the need to keep any records of customers
Sending all customer data to the regulator each day
Asking customers to check their own names against blacklists
Checking customers' names and aliases against blacklists with fuzzy matching
q.why: Fuzzy matching across huge data sets is far cheaper than traditional processing.

q.q: How can a bank use big data to improve its services?
o: Analysing emails, calls and social media for positive or negative feeling
Charging customers for every call they make to the call centre
Removing all online and mobile banking services for customers
Closing the branches that customers visit most often
q.why: Sentiment analysis reveals the causes of dissatisfaction.

q.q: How can big data provide early warning of illness?
o: Doctors no longer need to see any patients in person
Patterns in patient records spot serious illness early and identify who to screen
Wearable sensors cure illnesses as soon as they are detected in the data
Hospitals delete the records of all healthy patients each year
q.why: Spotting illness early means treatment is simpler and cheaper.

q.q: How do retailers use loyalty-card and transaction records?
o: To forecast demand by area and target offers at likely buyers
To check that customers' cards are not stolen
To decide which banks their customers should use
To set the wages of their store staff
q.why: This identifies potential customers and targets offers at those most likely to buy.

q.q: How does big data help medical research?
o: Predicting the share prices of drug companies for investors
Replacing clinical trials with surveys on social media
Choosing the best subjects for clinical trials and sharing trial data
Removing the need for patient consent in medical research
q.why: Better trial selection and data sharing speed up new cures.

q.q: How does big data make an organisation more competitive?
o: Less need to collect any data about customers
No need to follow data protection law
Better decisions, lower costs and happier customers
Fewer customers but higher prices for each one
q.why: The notes sum up competitiveness as better decisions, lower costs and happier customers.

q.q: How do retailers use social media data to forecast demand?
o: Staff read every social media post by hand and order stock to match
Social media companies set the retailer's prices for each product
Customers post their orders directly on social media for delivery
Algorithms comb posts and advertising data to spot which products will be in demand
q.why: Algorithms analyse posts and advertising data to predict trends.

q.q: Which data protection principle is breached when loyalty-card data is sold for an unrelated purpose?
o: Accuracy
Storage limitation
Purpose limitation
Data minimisation
q.why: Data collected for one purpose must not be reused for an incompatible one.

q.q: Why is anonymised data not always safe to release?
o: It must be deleted as soon as it is anonymised
It is always encrypted, so it cannot be analysed
It contains no information useful to anyone
Combining it with other data sets can re-identify individuals
q.why: Linking data sets, e.g. postcode, date of birth and gender, can single people out.

q.q: What is the main threat to privacy from data mining, according to the notes?
o: Personal data used for purposes the person has not agreed to or does not know about
Personal data being stored on paper files rather than on computer systems
Personal data being processed too slowly to be useful to the organisation
Personal data being deleted before it can be analysed for patterns
q.why: The main threat is use or sharing for purposes without the person's permission or knowledge.

q.q: A shop's analysis of purchases suggests a customer is pregnant before she has told anyone. Which privacy issue is this?
o: Purpose limitation
Re-identification
Sensitive inferences
Data breach
q.why: Mining can reveal sensitive facts people never disclosed.

q.q: A credit model penalises applicants from certain postcodes because the past data reflected bias. Which issue is this?
o: Surveillance
Storage limitation
Profiling and bias
Re-identification
q.why: Automated decisions may discriminate if the data reflects past bias.

q.q: Why are huge stores of personal data a security threat to privacy?
o: They can only be read by the person that each record describes
They are always stored without any passwords or encryption
They are attractive targets, so a breach could expose millions of records
They cannot be backed up in case of a hardware failure
q.why: Large stores of personal data attract attackers.

q.q: How can constant tracking, such as app location data, affect people?
o: It can change how people behave, a chilling effect
It guarantees people's data is accurate
It makes people's phones run more quickly
It stops data from being mined at all
q.why: Surveillance can change behaviour, known as a chilling effect.

q.q: Which law, alongside the UK GDPR, governs the processing of personal data in the UK?
o: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Freedom of Information Act 2000
Data Protection Act 2018
Computer Misuse Act 1990
q.why: Processing personal data is governed by the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

q.q: Which safeguard reduces the threat of data mining to privacy?
o: Collecting only the data that is needed
Removing human review of decisions
Keeping data for as long as possible
Selling data only to trusted partners
q.why: Data minimisation is one of the safeguards, along with anonymisation, transparency and security.

q.q: Why is transparency hard to achieve with data mining?
o: Data mining does not use personal data
Organisations are not allowed to tell people about mining
Complex analysis is hard to explain to the people whose data is used
People never want to know how their data is used
q.why: People must be told how their data will be used, but complex analysis is hard to explain.

q.q: Which best defines cloud computing?
o: Running a peer-to-peer network in which every computer shares its files
Using the internet to obtain, from a provider's server farms, services normally provided by a LAN
Using Bluetooth to share files between nearby devices with no servers
Storing an organisation's files on its own file server inside the building
q.why: Internet, a third-party provider, and services a LAN would otherwise provide.

q.q: What is a server farm?
o: A group of PCs sharing files peer to peer
A single file server that stores users' work
A centre containing a large number of linked servers
A wireless hotspot in a public place
q.why: Server farms are the physical home of cloud services.

q.q: Which deployment model is shared by many organisations?
o: On-premises server
Public cloud
Private cloud
Hosted solution
q.why: Public cloud resources are pooled between many tenants.

q.q: Who manages and processes an organisation's data in cloud computing?
o: The internet service provider of each user
The organisation's own network manager on its LAN
A third party, the cloud service provider
Each user, on their own device
q.why: Cloud data is managed and processed by the provider.

q.q: Which type of organisation is most likely to use a private cloud?
o: A small firm wanting the cheapest shared service
A home user storing holiday photos
A start-up with variable demand and little money
A bank with strict security and regulatory requirements
q.why: Private clouds suit organisations such as banks, health bodies and government.

q.q: What is a hybrid cloud?
o: A public cloud shared by many organisations at once
A private cloud hosted on dedicated hardware
A cloud that works without any internet connection
A private cloud or on-premises system linked to a public cloud
q.why: A hybrid cloud links private and public so data and applications can move between them.

q.q: A company rents virtual servers and storage from a cloud provider. Which service model is this?
o: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Platform as a service (PaaS)
Software as a service (SaaS)
Hosted solution
q.why: IaaS is renting virtual servers and storage.

q.q: A school uses web email and online office software through a browser. Which service model is this?
o: Platform as a service (PaaS)
Software as a service (SaaS)
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS)
Private cloud
q.why: SaaS delivers complete applications such as web email.

q.q: How do users normally reach a cloud service securely?
o: By downloading the provider's entire database onto their own PC first
Through a secure log-in, with data sent over an encrypted connection
By plugging a cable directly into the provider's server
Through an open Wi-Fi hotspot with no password or encryption
q.why: Secure log-in and encrypted connections protect access and data in transit.

q.q: How are cloud services usually paid for?
o: By a single payment when the servers are bought
By the number of employees in the organisation
They are always free to every organisation
By subscription or by use, with capacity on demand
q.why: Services are on demand and paid by subscription or use.

q.q: Which statement about where cloud data is stored is correct?
o: Users rarely know which server or even which country holds it
It is always stored on the user's local hard drive
It is stored on a single server chosen by the user
It is always stored in the user's own country
q.why: Data is not necessarily stored locally and its location is usually unknown to users.

q.q: What does virtualisation allow?
o: Several operating systems to run on one physical server at once
Users to log on to a server without passwords
A server to keep running without any electricity
One operating system to run across many physical servers at once
q.why: Many virtual servers, each with its own OS, share one physical host.

q.q: Which describes a hosted solution?
o: A group of servers acting as one system with load balancing
Hardware and software reserved for one client, paid for whether used or not
Resources shared dynamically between many clients as demand changes
A virtual server whose capacity grows automatically when demand spikes
q.why: A hosted solution is a dedicated, fixed allocation.

q.q: What is the purpose of clustering?
o: To reserve hardware for one client only
To copy data to a storage provider on a schedule
To divide one server into several virtual machines
To make several servers act as one system, sharing the load
q.why: Clustering gives load balancing, parallel processing and resilience.

q.q: What happens to a hosted instance when a client's demand spikes?
o: The instance is moved to a hosted solution
Extra capacity is allocated dynamically, with no downtime
The client must buy and install a new physical server
The instance stops until demand falls again
q.why: Every element of an instance is dynamic.

q.q: What software divides one physical server into several virtual machines?
o: An inference engine
A shell
A data warehouse
A hypervisor
q.why: A hypervisor creates the VMs, each with its own virtual processor, memory, disk and network card.

q.q: What is a hosted instance?
o: A block of a cloud server's resources acting as one client's own virtual server
A software imitation of a storage device that pools many disks
A group of servers that act together as one system with load balancing
A physical server and its software reserved entirely for one client
q.why: A hosted instance is a client's dynamic share of a cloud server.

q.q: A client in a hosted solution needs more capacity. What must it do?
o: Nothing, as capacity is added automatically
Pay to invest in more resources
Move its data to a hybrid cloud
Share its resources with other clients
q.why: Capacity in a hosted solution is not shared out dynamically.

q.q: Which suits a company with variable or growing demand?
o: A hosted instance
A hosted solution
A peer-to-peer network
A single dedicated server
q.why: Instances scale automatically and are paid for by use.

q.q: What is storage virtualisation?
o: Dividing one hard disk into many separate drives
Pooling many network storage devices so they appear as one
Copying data to a local USB drive
Storing data on virtual reality headsets
q.why: Storage virtualisation makes many devices appear as one resource.

q.q: What happens in a server cluster if one server fails?
o: The client must buy a replacement server
The other servers carry on with the work
All data held by the cluster is lost
The whole cluster stops until it is repaired
q.why: Clusters share work, so the others continue if one fails.

q.q: How does a client pay for a hosted instance compared with a hosted solution?
o: Both are paid for in full whether used or not
Both are free once the hardware is installed
An instance is paid for in full; a solution is paid for by use
An instance is paid for by use; a solution is paid for in full, used or not
q.why: Hosted instances charge for what is used; hosted solutions charge for everything allocated.

q.q: Which statement about a virtual machine is correct?
o: It must use the same operating system as every other VM
It runs its own operating system, unaware it shares the hardware
It can only run when no other VMs are running
It is a physical server reserved for one client
q.why: Each VM has its own virtual hardware, OS and applications.

q.q: Where is web-based email stored?
o: On the user's mobile phone SIM
In the PSTN exchange
On the service provider's servers
Only on the user's own laptop
q.why: That is why it can be read from any browser on any device.

q.q: What does an incremental backup copy?
o: Files changed since the last full backup
Only files that have been deleted
Files changed since the last backup of any kind
Every file, every time
q.why: A differential copies changes since the last full backup; an incremental since the last backup of any kind.

q.q: Which is an advantage of virtualised software for users?
o: It must be installed on every PC before it can be used
It works only when the computer is offline
It needs a dedicated server in each office
No installation is needed and updates reach everyone at once
q.why: It runs on the provider's servers and is delivered over the web.

q.q: How does cloud computing affect a PC's storage needs?
o: Storage needs are unchanged because files are kept in both places
Less local storage is needed because files and software are held remotely
More local storage is needed to hold copies of the cloud data
No local storage is needed at all, even for the operating system
q.why: Data and software move to remote servers, so the PC needs less local storage.

q.q: What does a differential backup copy?
o: Only files that have never been backed up
Every file on the system, every time
Only files changed since the last backup of any kind
All files changed since the last full backup
q.why: Differential copies all changes since the last full backup.

q.q: What is needed to restore from incremental backups?
o: Only the most recent incremental backup
The last full backup plus the latest incremental only
Every full backup ever made
The last full backup plus every incremental since
q.why: Incrementals are fastest to make but slowest to restore.

q.q: What is needed to restore from differential backups?
o: The last full backup plus every differential since
Only the latest differential backup
The last full backup plus the latest differential
Every differential backup ever made
q.why: Each differential holds all changes since the last full backup.

q.q: What is the main trade-off of moving files and software to the cloud?
o: Dependence on the internet connection to reach them
Software must be installed and updated on each PC
Much greater need for local storage space
Files can only be opened on one device
q.why: Without a connection, files and applications may not be available.

q.q: How does a remotely hosted application let staff at many branches use it?
o: It runs on a server in the head office with no internet access at all
Each branch keeps its own separate copy of the data and the software
It runs on a remote server as an instance on a virtual desktop reached from anywhere
It is installed separately on every PC in every branch
q.why: Business software and data sit on the provider's server and many staff can use them at once.

q.q: How does cloud backup by syncing work?
o: Files are copied to a local USB drive each evening
Every change is backed up automatically as it is made
The whole system is copied once a month on a schedule
Only files that are deleted are copied to the provider
q.why: Syncing backs up each change automatically to the storage provider.

q.q: How does the cloud provide data storage?
o: Data is saved on a file server inside the organisation's own building
Data is saved off-site on a third party's remote database reached over the internet
Data is saved on the computer's own hard drive and shared by Bluetooth
Data is saved on each user's phone and synchronised by text message
q.why: Cloud storage is off-site, remote and run by a third party.

q.q: Which is a drawback of cloud computing?
o: Dependence on internet connectivity
No upfront cost for hardware
Scalability to meet changing demand
Access to files from anywhere
q.why: No connection, or a provider outage, means no access.

q.q: Which is a security issue specific to cloud computing?
o: Users must install the provider's software on every machine they use
Updates take longer to reach each user than with a LAN
Provider staff with access could misuse data without being detected
Files cannot be shared between staff at different sites
q.why: Insider threats at the provider are a cloud-specific concern.

q.q: Why are cloud systems an attractive target for cyberattacks?
o: They hold huge amounts of many organisations' data in one place
They are never protected by passwords or encryption
They are only used by small, unprotected firms
They are always run by inexperienced staff
q.why: Concentrating data from many organisations makes an attractive target.

q.q: Data held by a cloud provider in another country could be accessed by that country's government. Which security issue is this?
o: Trust in updates
Confidentiality
Availability
Insider threat
q.why: Data held abroad may be legally accessed by that country's government or surveillance programmes.

q.q: After a data breach at a cloud provider, who usually remains the data controller under UK data protection law?
o: The government of the country holding the data
The business that put its data in the cloud
The individual customers whose data was taken
The cloud provider that stores the data
q.why: It can be unclear who is liable, but the business usually remains the data controller.

q.q: How does cloud computing make disaster recovery simpler and cheaper?
o: All data is kept on one server in the business's own office
Staff no longer need to log in to access the business's data
Data can be mirrored at several redundant sites by the provider
Backups are printed out and stored in a fireproof safe
q.why: Mirroring at redundant sites simplifies backup, recovery and business continuity.

q.q: Which is a business benefit of cloud computing?
o: Data is always stored in the business's own country
The business keeps full physical control of all its servers
The business no longer depends on any internet connection
Staff can collaborate from many locations on the same files
q.why: Collaboration from many locations and devices is a key benefit.

q.q: Why is the statement 'the cloud is not secure' unlikely to gain credit?
o: It is too vague; a specific risk and how to manage it is needed
It is untrue, as cloud data can never be accessed by attackers
Examiners only credit points about cost, not security
It describes a business benefit rather than a security issue
q.why: The notes say to explain the specific risk, such as data held abroad, and its management.
